name.text: WAT 10.1: Brace Yourself, It's a Map!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write five functions that build a Python dict, read it, add to it and report its contents.

How this works in Python

Java's HashMap wants a declaration, a constructor, and a method call for every job you give it.

Map<String, Integer> readings = new HashMap<>();
readings.put("north-pier", 14);
readings.put("kaitaia", 21);

int north = readings.get("north-pier");
boolean known = readings.containsKey("kaitaia");

for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> entry : readings.entrySet()) {
    System.out.println(entry.getKey() + " " + entry.getValue());
}

Python's version of that map is a dict, short for dictionary. It is built into the language, so there is nothing to import and no type to declare.

The literal

Braces hold comma-separated key: value pairs, and a colon separates each key from its value. That one line replaces the constructor and both calls to put.

readings = {"north-pier": 14, "kaitaia": 21}

Lookup

Square brackets read a key, so readings["kaitaia"] hands back 21. They are the same brackets you put on a list in the lists topic, with a key in place of a position. What happens when the key is absent is the whole subject of the next question, so every lookup you write below asks for a key you know is there.

Assignment

The same brackets on the left of an = store a value. readings["cape-reinga"] = 19 adds the key when it is absent and replaces the value when it is present. One piece of syntax covers put.

Membership

"kaitaia" in readings is True or False, and it tests keys, never values. It replaces containsKey, and it is the same in you used on a list. Python has no has_key method, because the language grew the operator instead.

Iteration

readings.items() hands you one (key, value) pair each pass, and a loop header naming two variables unpacks that pair for you. That is the unpacking from the tuples topic doing the work of entrySet and both getters at once.

for station, celsius in readings.items():
    print(station, celsius)

Order

Here is the part that catches Java developers out. A HashMap returns its entries in whatever order hashing produced, and the documentation warns you not to depend on it. A Python dict keeps the order the keys went in. That behaviour arrived as an implementation detail in CPython 3.6 and became a promise of the language itself in Python 3.7, so you can rely on it. There is no LinkedHashMap to reach for, because the plain dict already does that job.

Replacing the value under a key that is already present leaves the key where it sits, so the order does not shift. len(readings) counts the entries, the same len you called on a string and on a list.

Your task

Write five functions. None of them prints.

  • make_readings() takes no arguments and returns the dict {"north-pier": 14, "kaitaia": 21}, written as one literal.
  • reading_for(readings, station) returns the value stored under station. The tests only ask for keys that are present.
  • record(readings, station, celsius) stores celsius under station and returns nothing at all. The caller keeps hold of the dict, so change the one you were handed rather than building a new one.
  • knows(readings, station) returns whether station is a key.
  • report(readings) returns one string holding station=celsius for every entry, separated by a single space, in the order the keys went in. Walk the pairs with .items(), then join the pieces with the join method from the strings topic.

An empty dict has nothing to report, so report({}) returns the empty string.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Build the dict with one literal. An empty {} followed by two assignments is put wearing a disguise.
  • Ask with in. There is no containsKey and no has_key.
  • Walk the pairs with .items(). Do not loop over .keys() and subscript each one, because that pays for the lookup twice.
  • sorted() appears nowhere in your answer. Insertion order is the lesson.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: readings = make_readings() print(readings) print(reading_for(readings, "kaitaia")) print(knows(readings, "kaitaia"), knows(readings, "cape-reinga"))
readings = make_readings() record(readings, "cape-reinga", 19) print(readings) record(readings, "north-pier", 15) print(readings) print(report(readings)) print(record(readings, "raglan", 18))

import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (make_readings, reading_for, record, knows, report)) assert "sorted(" not in whole, "rule broken: insertion order is the lesson, do not sort" assert ".keys()" not in whole, "rule broken: walk the pairs with .items()" assert ".items()" in inspect.getsource(report), "rule broken: walk the pairs with .items()" assert " in " in inspect.getsource(knows), "rule broken: ask with the in operator" assert "{" in inspect.getsource(make_readings), "rule broken: build the dict with one literal" empty = {} print(repr(report(empty)), len(empty), knows(empty, "kaitaia")) fresh = {} record(fresh, "b", 2) record(fresh, "a", 1) record(fresh, "b", 3) print(fresh, len(fresh)) print(report(fresh))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four functions that read a configuration dict and tell a missing key apart from a stored None.

How this works in Python

Java's Map answers a missing key with null. That one habit shapes every lookup you have ever written.

Integer port = config.get("port");
if (port == null) {
    port = 8080;
}

if (config.containsKey("host")) {
    connect(config.get("host"));
}

Python splits that one behaviour into two forms. A dict is Python's hash map, written with braces as {"port": 8080}. Square brackets are the strict form, and reading with square brackets is called a subscript. config["port"] returns the value, and a missing key raises KeyError instead of handing back nothing.

The forgiving form is a method. config.get("port") returns None when the key is absent, which is the behaviour your Java reflex expects. None is Python's null. Pass a second argument and you pick the fallback yourself, so config.get("timeout", 30) returns 30 when timeout is absent.

config.setdefault("retries", 3) does two jobs in one call. It returns the stored value when the key exists. It stores 3 and returns 3 when the key does not exist. The dict grows by one entry.

Your containsKey then get pair costs two hash lookups. It also leaves a gap between the check and the read. Python closes both with a single call, so never write if key in config followed by config[key]. The word in is still worth knowing, because "port" in config tests keys and reads well on its own.

Python names this style EAFP, short for "easier to ask forgiveness than permission". You run the operation and you catch the failure. The Java habit of testing first has a name too, "look before you leap", and Python prefers the other one.

Three Python keywords cover the Java syntax you already use. try is Java's try. except is Java's catch. raise is Java's throw. Each header ends in a colon, and the indented lines under it are the block.

try:
    value = config["port"]
except KeyError as exc:
    raise RuntimeError("no port") from exc

except KeyError as exc catches the error and binds it to the name exc. raise ... from exc chains the new error to the original one. That line is Python's version of new RuntimeException(msg, cause). The original KeyError stays reachable afterwards as exc.__cause__.

To walk a dict, call .items(). Each pass of the loop hands you a key and a value together. The header names both, so it is the for loop from the loops topic with the unpacking from the tuples topic in front of the in.

for key, value in config.items():
    print(key, value)

Do not loop over the keys and then subscript each one. That costs two lookups per entry and repeats the habit this exercise removes.

One trap is left, and Java has the same one. containsKey(k) and get(k) != null disagree whenever a key is present with a null value. In Python, config.get("label") returns None for an absent key and also for a key whose stored value is None. Those two cases are indistinguishable.

The repair is a sentinel. object() creates a bare object equal to nothing but itself. Store one in a module-level name and pass it as the default.

_MISSING = object()
value = config.get(key, _MISSING)

value is _MISSING is then true only when the key was absent. The leading underscore is a Python naming convention meaning "private to this module". It is a hint to readers, not an access modifier.

Your task

Write four functions. The sentinel is already in the answer box.

  • read_settings(cfg) reads port with square brackets, timeout with .get and a default of 30, and retries with setdefault and a default of 3. It returns the three values as a tuple in that order, which a bare comma-separated return builds for you. Calling it grows cfg by one key.
  • config_table(cfg) returns one string holding one line per entry. Each line is the key left-aligned in ten characters, then the value. Walk the dict with .items(), then join the lines with \n using the join method from the strings topic.
  • must_get(cfg, key) returns cfg[key]. When the key is absent, it raises RuntimeError chained from the original KeyError. For the key nope, the message reads device config is missing 'nope'.
  • lookup(cfg, key) returns the string ABSENT when the key is absent, the string NULL when the stored value is None, and the value itself otherwise.

The quotes in the must_get message come from the !r conversion you met in the strings topic. The field width in config_table is the {key:<10} spec from that same topic.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character, spaces included.

Rules
  • Never write if key in cfg and then cfg[key]. That is containsKey in disguise, and one lookup does the work of two.
  • Tell absent apart from None with the sentinel. .get(key) or default is banned, because the truthiness topic showed it also fires on 0, "" and an empty list.
  • Let no KeyError escape uncaught. Never catch one with a bare except:.
  • Walk the dict with .items(). Do not loop over the keys and subscript each one.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: cfg = {"port": 8080, "label": None} print(cfg.get("label"), cfg.get("nope")) print(lookup(cfg, "port")) print(lookup(cfg, "label")) print(lookup(cfg, "nope")) print(must_get(cfg, "port")) try: must_get(cfg, "nope") except RuntimeError as exc: print(exc) print(type(exc.__cause__).__name__)

expected.text: None None 8080 NULL ABSENT 8080 device config is missing 'nope' KeyError

testcode.text: import inspect import re whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (read_settings, config_table, must_get, lookup)) assert not re.search(r"if\s+\w+\s+in\s+\w+\s*:", whole), "rule broken: no look-before-you-leap" assert not re.search(r"\.get\([^)]*\)\s*or\b", whole), "rule broken: no .get(...) or default" assert "except:" not in whole, "rule broken: no bare except" assert "setdefault(" in whole, "rule broken: use setdefault" assert ".items()" in inspect.getsource(config_table), "rule broken: iterate .items()" assert ".keys()" not in whole, "rule broken: no .keys() then subscript" assert type(_MISSING) is object, "rule broken: _MISSING must be object()" blank = {"a": None} print(lookup(blank, "a"), lookup(blank, "b"), lookup(blank, "a") is None) grown = {} print(read_settings({"port": 1, "timeout": 0})) print(config_table(grown) == "")

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write five functions that group and count fault records with defaultdict and Counter.

How this works in Python

Grouping and counting each take one line in Java.

Map<String, List<String>> groups = new HashMap<>();
groups.computeIfAbsent(subsystem, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(code);

Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
counts.merge(code, 1, Integer::sum);

The JDK ships no multiset, so teams add an outside collections library when they want one. Python ships both jobs in its standard library, in a module named collections.

An import brings a name into your file. It is Java's import with the module written after from and the names written after import. Write it once, at the top.

from collections import Counter, defaultdict

defaultdict(list) is a dict that builds a missing value instead of raising. You hand it a factory. list with no brackets after it is the list type itself, so Python calls it with no arguments to get a new empty list. Read that as ArrayList::new rather than as a call. Reading a missing key calls the factory, stores the result and returns it.

groups = defaultdict(list)
groups["radar"].append("E14")

That is computeIfAbsent with the lambda deleted. One difference matters, and it is the point of this exercise. computeIfAbsent inserts only when you call it. A defaultdict inserts on any read of a missing key, including a read you believed was harmless. Reading a container and changing its size is a defect few reviewers catch.

Counter is a dict whose values are counts. Hand it any sequence and it tallies the items.

counts = Counter(["E14", "E02", "E14"])
print(counts["E14"])   # 2
print(counts["E99"])   # 0

Reading a missing key returns 0 and stores nothing at all. The Counter's length does not move. That is the opposite of defaultdict, and the two live in the same module.

counts.most_common(2) returns the two highest tallies as a list of (item, count) pairs, highest first.

One pair of names still needs care. dict.update(other) replaces values, the same as Map.putAll. Counter.update(other) adds them. Same method name, opposite arithmetic.

Your task

Write five functions. records is a list of (subsystem, code) pairs, so a loop header of for subsystem, code in records unpacks both names at once.

  • group_faults(records) returns a defaultdict(list) mapping each subsystem to its codes, in the order the records arrive.
  • tally_codes(records) returns a Counter of the codes.
  • top_two(counts) returns the two most common entries.
  • merge_report(base, extra) takes two plain dicts and returns a pair. The first item is a Counter built from base and updated with extra, so the counts add. The second is a plain dict built from base and updated with extra, so the values are replaced. Neither result may change base, and building a new container from base leaves base alone.
  • probe(groups, counts, key) returns three tuples in order. The first holds the length of each container before you read anything. The second holds the value read from each container under key. The third holds the length of each container again. The tests pass a key that is in neither container, so the first and third tuples show you which container grew.

Printing a defaultdict shows its factory, so expect defaultdict(<class 'list'>, {...}) rather than plain braces. Wrap it in dict(...) when you want the tidy form.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • The word if may not appear anywhere in your answer. The container decides what a missing key means.
  • Initialise no key by hand. No d[k] = [] before the append, and no pre-seeding pass.
  • Count with a Counter. += 1 is banned.
  • Make the lengths from probe prove which of your two containers inserts on a read and which does not.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: records = [ ("radar", "E14"), ("power", "E02"), ("radar", "E14"), ("power", "E77"), ("radar", "E02"), ("radar", "E14"), ] groups = group_faults(records) print(dict(groups)) print(groups) counts = tally_codes(records) print(counts) print(top_two(counts))

import inspect import re whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (group_faults, tally_codes, top_two, merge_report, probe)) assert not re.search(r"\bif\b", whole), "rule broken: the word if is banned" assert "+= 1" not in whole, "rule broken: count with a Counter" assert "] = []" not in whole and "] = 0" not in whole, "rule broken: no hand-initialised keys" assert "defaultdict(" in whole, "rule broken: use defaultdict" assert ".most_common(" in whole, "rule broken: use most_common" records = [("radar", "E14"), ("power", "E02")] groups = group_faults(records) counts = tally_codes(records) print(probe(groups, counts, "engine")) print(dict(groups)) print(counts)

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write six functions that show which dict keys collapse into one and what a keys view will let you do.

How this works in Python

Put three keys in a Java HashMap and you get three entries.

Map<Object, String> m = new HashMap<>();
m.put(1, "int one");
m.put(1.0, "float one");
m.put(Boolean.TRUE, "bool true");
// m.size() == 3

Integer.equals(Double) is false whatever the numbers are, and Boolean is a third type again. Python disagrees on every count. 1 == 1.0 is true, True == 1 is true, and bool is a subclass of int in which True is 1.

A dict key needs two properties. It must support hash(), and equal objects must hash the same. That is the hashCode and equals contract you already know. Python honours it, so those three keys collapse into one entry.

Which key survives, and which value? Assigning to a key that is already present overwrites the value and leaves the key object alone. The first key object stays. The last value wins. Looping over a dict gives its keys, so list(d) hands you those keys in insertion order.

Only hashable objects may be keys. A tuple is the fixed sequence written with commas that you met in the tuples topic, and a tuple is hashable when its contents are. A list is mutable and is not hashable, so hash([1, 2]) raises TypeError. Python declares this on the type itself. list.__hash__ is None, where tuple.__hash__ is a real function.

A tuple key is how you build a composite key. Java would glue row + "," + col into a string. Do not do that here.

grid = {(0, 0): "nw", (0, 1): "ne"}
print(grid[0, 1])   # ne

The subscript needs no inner brackets. A comma inside [...] already builds a tuple, as you saw in the tuples topic.

Python dicts keep insertion order, so there is no separate LinkedHashMap to reach for. Overwriting a key leaves that key where it sits. Deleting a key and then re-inserting it sends the key to the end.

del config[key] removes an entry in place. Deleting while you iterate the same dict raises RuntimeError with the message dictionary changed size during iteration. Java throws ConcurrentModificationException here, so the shape is familiar. Take a snapshot first with list(config.items()), then delete from the dict while you walk the copy.

config.keys() returns a view. A view is a live window on the dict, not a copy. Insert a key and the view you are already holding shows it. Java's keySet is live too, but it writes through, so keySet().remove(k) deletes the entry. A Python view is read-only and has no remove at all. It does support in and the set operators.

Your task

Write six functions.

  • collapse() takes no arguments. Build an empty dict, then assign to 1, 1.0 and True in that order, with the values int one, float one and bool true. Return the dict, its length, the surviving key, and the name of that key's type. type(x).__name__ gives you the name.
  • grid_lookup(grid) returns the entry at row 0, column 1, read with no inner brackets.
  • hash_report() takes no arguments. It returns list.__hash__ and the text of the TypeError that hash([1, 2]) raises. Catch that error with try and except, the way you caught KeyError earlier in this topic. str(exc) gives you the text.
  • prune(config) deletes every entry whose value is FAIL, in place, then stores PASS under the key status. It returns the resulting keys as a list.
  • live_view(config) takes the keys view and copies it into a list. It then inserts the key added with the value 0. It returns the copy and the view object itself. Printing both shows you what a live view does.
  • view_powers(config) returns whether the view has a remove attribute, whether alpha is in the view, and the view intersected with {"alpha"}. hasattr(obj, "name") answers the first one.

The caller keeps hold of config, so prune must change the dict it was handed. status starts out as a failure, so prune deletes it and then stores it again. Watch where that key lands in the returned order.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Build composite keys from tuples. A "row,col" string is a Java workaround for a problem Python does not have. Stringify nothing to make it hashable.
  • Never delete from the container you are iterating. Snapshot the keys with list() first, or take the RuntimeError.
  • Prune in place. Do not build a replacement dict, because the caller is holding this one.
  • Do not call .remove() on a keys view. Find out instead what the view will and will not let you do.
  • sorted() appears nowhere in your answer. Insertion order is the whole lesson.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: config = {"alpha": "PASS", "beta": "FAIL", "gamma": "PASS", "status": "FAIL"} print(prune(config)) print(config) before, after = live_view({"a": 1, "b": 2}) print(before) print(after) print(view_powers({"alpha": 1, "beta": 2}))

import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (collapse, grid_lookup, hash_report, prune, live_view, view_powers)) assert "sorted(" not in whole, "rule broken: no sorted()" assert "list(" in inspect.getsource(prune), "rule broken: snapshot the keys with list()" assert "del " in inspect.getsource(prune), "rule broken: delete in place" assert "return {" not in whole, "rule broken: do not build a replacement dict" assert "[0, 1]" in inspect.getsource(grid_lookup), "rule broken: read grid[0, 1] with no inner brackets" assert "str(" not in inspect.getsource(grid_lookup), "rule broken: composite keys are tuples" assert ".remove(" not in whole, "rule broken: do not call remove on a keys view" held = {"beta": "FAIL", "status": "FAIL"} same = held print(prune(held), same, same is held) d, size, survivor, kind = collapse() print(d[True], d[1.0], size, survivor, kind) victim = {"x": 1, "y": 2} try: for key in victim: del victim[key] except RuntimeError as exc: print(exc)

expected.text: ['status'] {'status': 'PASS'} True bool true bool true 1 1 int dictionary changed size during iteration

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write five functions that answer permission questions with the set operators and key a dict with a frozenset.

How this works in Python

Java set algebra is a run of mutating calls on a defensive copy.

Set<String> missing = new HashSet<>(required);
missing.removeAll(granted);
Set<String> overlap = new HashSet<>(required);
overlap.retainAll(granted);
boolean covered = granted.containsAll(required);
boolean apart = Collections.disjoint(required, granted);

Python gives each of those an operator, and every operator returns a new set. Nothing changes in place, so you need no defensive copy.

  • a - b is difference, the members of a that are not in b.
  • a & b is intersection.
  • a | b is union.
  • a ^ b is symmetric difference, the members in one set but not in both.
  • a <= b asks whether every member of a is in b. That is b.containsAll(a) read the other way round.
  • a.isdisjoint(b) replaces Collections.disjoint(a, b).

A set literal is a comma-separated run of values in braces, so {"read", "write"} is a set of two strings. That notation holds one trap, and every Python beginner meets it once. {} is an empty dict, not an empty set, because dicts claimed the braces first. Write set() when you want an empty set. Java's Set.of() has no such trap.

A set is unordered and its members must be hashable. That is the same rule you met for dict keys earlier in this topic. Printing a set of several strings gives no order you can rely on, so the tests sort before they print.

A frozenset is the immutable version of a set. Being immutable makes it hashable, so a frozenset can be a dict key where a plain set cannot. Java lets you use a HashSet as a map key and trusts you not to change it. Python refuses the mutable one instead. A list cannot be a key either, and table[["read"]] = "x" raises TypeError with the text unhashable type: 'list'. Two frozensets holding the same members are equal and hash the same, so the order you built them in does not affect a lookup.

Java reaches for LinkedHashSet when it wants uniqueness and order together. Python has no ordered set. Use a dict, because dict keys are unique and dicts keep insertion order. dict.fromkeys(tags) builds a dict whose keys are the tags in first-seen order, and list(...) turns those keys back into a list.

Your task

Write five functions.

  • audit(required, granted) returns four values in this order. The required permissions that were not granted. The granted permissions that were not required. The overlap. And whether granted covers required. Use one operator for each.
  • conflicts(a, b) returns whether the two sets share nothing, and their symmetric difference.
  • dedupe(tags) returns a list with duplicates removed and first-seen order kept.
  • role_table() takes no arguments. Build a dict with the frozenset of read and write as its key and editor as its value. Then try to store a value under the list ["read", "write"] and catch the TypeError. Return the value looked up by an equal frozenset built in the opposite order, and the text of the error.
  • empty_set() takes no arguments. It returns an empty set and the name of the type of {}.

The tests compare dedupe exactly, so return a list and not a set.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • No for. No if. No len(). The set operators answer all four of the audit questions on their own.
  • Use the operators, not .union(), .intersection(), .difference() or .issubset(). .isdisjoint() is the one method you need.
  • {} will not give you an empty set. Get that right on the first attempt.
  • Keep first-seen order in dedupe, and return a list.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: disjoint, symmetric = conflicts({"a", "b"}, {"b", "c"}) print(disjoint, sorted(symmetric)) apart, both = conflicts({"read"}, {"deploy"}) print(apart, sorted(both)) print(dedupe(["radar", "power", "radar", "engine", "power"])) print(dedupe([])) print(role_table()) print(empty_set())

import inspect import re whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (audit, conflicts, dedupe, role_table, empty_set)) assert not re.search(r"\bfor\b", whole), "rule broken: no for" assert not re.search(r"\bif\b", whole), "rule broken: no if" assert "len(" not in whole, "rule broken: no len()" for banned in (".union(", ".intersection(", ".difference(", ".issubset(", ".symmetric_difference("): assert banned not in whole, "rule broken: use the operators, not the named methods" assert "<=" in inspect.getsource(audit), "rule broken: use the subset operator" assert "fromkeys" in inspect.getsource(dedupe), "rule broken: dedupe with dict.fromkeys" assert "frozenset(" in inspect.getsource(role_table), "rule broken: use a frozenset key" print(audit(set(), set())) print(dedupe(["a", "a", "a"]), type(dedupe(["a"])).__name__) print(empty_set()[0] == set(), empty_set()[0] == {})

expected.text: (set(), set(), set(), True) ['a'] list True False
